research_text:
## Factual research brief

### 1. Governed API and meaning of the reported value

`java.security.KeyPairGenerator` is the JCA engine for generating public/private key pairs. It is obtained through `getInstance(...)`, initialized either with a key-size/default parameter set or an algorithm-specific `AlgorithmParameterSpec`, and produces a `KeyPair` through `generateKeyPair()` or `genKeyPair()`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

For the supplied CrySL rule, the reported message:

> expecting one of RSA, EC, DSA, DiffieHellman, DH but found ECDH

refers specifically to the **first `String` argument named `algorithm` in the rule’s `Get` event**—that is, a matched `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance(algorithm)` or `getInstance(algorithm, _)` call. It is not a reported value from `initialize(...)`, `generateKeyPair()`, a generated `KeyPair`, or `KeyAgreement`. The rule’s first constraint requires that captured string to be in its five-value allowlist. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

The Java SE standard-name specification distinguishes the two service types:

* **`EC`** is the standard `KeyPairGenerator` algorithm name for elliptic-curve key-pair generation.
* **`ECDH`** is the standard `KeyAgreement` algorithm name for elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman key agreement—not a listed `KeyPairGenerator` algorithm name. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

The Oracle JDK’s SunEC provider documentation makes the same distinction: it lists `EC` under `KeyPairGenerator`, and `ECDH` under `KeyAgreement`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/pls/topic/lookup?ctx=javase25&id=security_guide_jdk_providers))

This does **not** establish that every provider must reject `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("ECDH")`: Java SE permits providers to support additional, non-standard algorithms, and `getInstance` succeeds when a selected provider supplies the requested service. The standard-name specification and JCA API do not make the CrySL allowlist an exhaustive list of all provider-defined names. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

### 2. Officially documented usage and remediation guidance

Official JCA documentation describes these relevant usage rules:

* Request a `KeyPairGenerator` with a standard algorithm name through `getInstance(...)`; the chosen provider is the first suitable registered provider unless a provider is explicitly selected. A missing implementation produces `NoSuchAlgorithmException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
* Use algorithm-independent initialization with a key size, or algorithm-specific initialization with an `AlgorithmParameterSpec`. Key-size meaning and supported values are algorithm- and provider-specific. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
* Do not rely on uninitialized-generator defaults where reproducibility or portability matters. The `KeyPairGenerator` documentation explicitly says that defaults vary between providers and may change in future versions, and **recommends explicit initialization**. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
* For general-purpose applications, Oracle’s provider documentation recommends not pinning a particular provider unless necessary, because provider-specific availability and optimization vary across Java implementations. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/pls/topic/lookup?ctx=javase25&id=security_guide_jdk_providers))

For elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman specifically, the documented service separation is:

* Generate an EC key pair through the `KeyPairGenerator` service using the `EC` key-pair-generation algorithm.
* Perform the agreement operation through the `KeyAgreement` service using `ECDH`; `KeyAgreement` documents that key-agreement keys may be created by `KeyPairGenerator`, among other mechanisms. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

**Documented remediation limits:** the Oracle API documentation does not contain a finding-specific remediation instruction such as “replace `ECDH` with `EC`” for an arbitrary reported call. Its concrete recommendation is to use the standard name appropriate to the requested engine and to initialize `KeyPairGenerator` explicitly rather than depend on provider defaults. It also documents `NoSuchAlgorithmException` if the selected provider lacks the requested `KeyPairGenerator` implementation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

No exact initialization arguments, selected provider, curve/domain parameters, or generated-key consumer were supplied. Therefore, the official sources do not determine which parameter set or provider behavior applies to the reported usage.

### 3. Compatibility, persisted/wire formats, platform support, and migration

**Persisted and transmitted keys.** The `Key` API documents that encoded keys use a standard external representation when needed outside the JVM, including transmission to another party. It gives `X.509` `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` as the typical public-key format and `PKCS#8` `PrivateKeyInfo` as the typical private-key format. It also advises that a serialized `Key` should use `KeyRep`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))

**What is not documented.** The reviewed `KeyPairGenerator`, standard-names, and `Key` documentation does **not** promise that changing a `KeyPairGenerator` algorithm name, provider, explicit initialization, curve, or provider default preserves:

* identical `getEncoded()` bytes;
* a pre-existing persisted key’s encoding or associated parameters;
* compatibility with a particular external wire protocol; or
* compatibility with an undisclosed remote peer or key consumer.

The standard encoding formats alone do not constitute a documented compatibility guarantee for a changed generator configuration. The sources instead identify encoding and conversion mechanisms: `KeyFactory` can construct keys from key specifications and supports compatible key specifications such as `X509EncodedKeySpec`; that is an API capability, not a documented `ECDH`-to-`EC` migration procedure. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))

**Platform/version support.**

* `KeyPairGenerator` itself has existed since Java 1.1. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
* `ECGenParameterSpec`, the standard specification class for named EC domain parameters, has existed since Java 1.5. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/ECGenParameterSpec.html))
* In the reviewed Java SE 25 documentation, every implementation is required to support `KeyPairGenerator` algorithm `EC` for `secp256r1` and `secp384r1`, while `KeyAgreement` is separately required to support `ECDH` for those curves. The documentation directs users to release documentation for additional implementation support. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
* For the Oracle JDK 25 SunEC provider specifically, `EC` `KeyPairGenerator` accepts sizes 256, 384, or 521 and defaults to 384; this is provider documentation, not a Java SE-wide guarantee. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/pls/topic/lookup?ctx=javase25&id=security_guide_jdk_providers))

**Migration path.** No official, generic migration path was found in the reviewed API sources for changing a `KeyPairGenerator` request from a provider-specific or non-standard name to a standard one. The documented information is limited to standard service names, provider-dependent support, initialization behavior, standard key encodings, and `KeyFactory` conversion APIs. Compatibility must therefore remain unresolved without the actual provider/version, initialization parameters, persisted representation, and consumer/protocol requirements.

### 4. Exact CrySL rule matching and condition

Source reviewed:  
`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl`

The rule declares exactly one governed API type:

```text
SPEC java.security.KeyPairGenerator
```

Its event matching declarations are, verbatim:

```text
g1: getInstance(algorithm);
g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
Get := g1 | g2;

i1: initialize(keysize);
i2: initialize(keysize, _);
i3: initialize(params);
i4: initialize(params, _);
Init := i1 | i2 | i3 | i4;

k1: keyPair = generateKeyPair();
k2: keyPair = genKeyPair();
Gen := k1 | k2;
```

The source binds `algorithm` as `java.lang.String`, `keysize` as `int`, and `params` as `java.security.spec.AlgorithmParameterSpec`. Thus, it constrains the call shape by declared argument count and bound-object form:

* `getInstance`: one argument, or two arguments with the second represented by `_`;
* `initialize`: one argument or two arguments, in either a `keysize` or `params` form;
* `generateKeyPair` and `genKeyPair`: zero arguments, with result bound as `keyPair`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

The rule’s required event order is, verbatim:

```text
Get, Init, Gen
```

The exact condition that produces the supplied “expecting one of … but found ECDH” class of message is, verbatim:

```text
algorithm in {"RSA", "EC", "DSA", "DiffieHellman", "DH"};
```

The rule additionally declares these algorithm-dependent key-size constraints:

```text
algorithm in {"RSA"} => keysize in {4096, 3072};
algorithm in {"DSA"} => keysize in {3072};
algorithm in {"DiffieHellman", "DH"} => keysize in {3072};
algorithm in {"EC"} => keysize in {256};
```

and corresponding `preparedRSA`, `preparedDSA`, `preparedDH`, and `preparedEC` required predicates for `params`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

**Can it match a method that merely shares one of these names? No, not under the rule declaration as written.** The source declares `SPEC java.security.KeyPairGenerator`; it does not declare a name-only rule, nor does it name any second receiver type. The event clauses themselves contain method names and argument patterns, but the only governed API type in the source is `java.security.KeyPairGenerator`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

### Source limitations and unresolved questions

* The CrySL URL is on the moving `master` branch. The reviewed text was not tied to a specific repository commit, and the supplied SHA-256 was not independently verified against the fetched source.
* The reported detector output alone does not identify the exact resolved call, selected provider, JDK/runtime version, initialization path, EC parameter set, generated-key encoding, persistence mechanism, or key consumer.
* The reviewed official documentation does not provide a generic migration guarantee for existing keys or peer interoperability when generator configuration changes.
* This brief reports API semantics and source text only; it does not assess a deployment, infer repository behavior, or prescribe a code change.
